1.pericope_label: The mighty God, even the Lord, hath spoken, and called the earth from the rising of the sun unto the going down thereof... He shall call to the heavens from above, and to the earth, that he may judge his people

schools.summary: Handles the opening as a formal proclamation. The three divine names have been variously construed, and while the Authorised Version follows two ancient Greek translators in running them together, the Masoretic accents favour taking each as a separate appellative — a stiffness admitted and defended as deliberate, since the poet is imitating a royal edict, and since the monarch is divine the range runs not territorially but from sunrise to sunset. The change of tense at the third verse marks the moment the vision opens; and the summons of heaven and earth is read as the calling of witnesses, a second voice rejecting the alternative that they are themselves told to gather the saints, since gathering is no work of theirs.

States the psalm's theme before expounding it: there have always been hypocrites who placed religion in a mere observance of ceremonies, and the psalm exposes the dishonour done to God by confounding ceremony with religion, showing that his worship is spiritual and consists of prayer and thanksgiving. On the authorship it notes that the particle prefixed to Asaph's name admits two renderings, leaving it doubtful whether he wrote the psalms or merely received them to be sung. A second voice takes the divine title of Christ and rules out both his first coming, which was silent, and his last.

Treats Asaph as almost certainly the author, being of high repute and named second to David as a composer, and reports the stylistic verdict that these psalms are stiffer and more obscure than David's. Notices how abruptly the poem opens. A second voice in this school hears the worshippers themselves speaking the third verse, observes that though he is our God he comes to execute judgment upon us, and takes the summons of heaven and earth as the calling of angels and men to witness the equity of the proceedings.

Reads the scene as a court being convened, the original contract between God and Israel restated, and all the earth called to attend because at the last all nations shall be gathered to hear their doom; adds that when God speaks his own people should give ear, for who will if they do not. Presses the preposition in the second verse: the majesty of God is most conspicuous among his elect but not confined to them, for the church is not a dark lantern but a candlestick, and he shines not only in Zion but out of her.

Identifies the speaker rather than describing the scene. Not any man nor any angel has spoken but the God of gods, and he who called the world from sunrise to sunset is Christ, the Word made flesh, by whom all things were made — so that if any were made gods, by him they were made. The exposition opens by demanding that each reader set his conscience without deceit before his eyes, since God flatters no one.

debates.question: Did Asaph write the psalms that bear his name?

positions.summary: Most probably yes, on the strength of his standing as a composer and seer.
Probably, but the prefixed particle leaves open that the psalms were merely delivered to him by David to be sung.

debates.question: How should the three divine names of the first verse be construed?

positions.summary: As separate appellatives, on the Masoretic accents; the resulting stiffness is deliberate, imitating a royal proclamation.
As a stacked royal style, the titles massed at the front as in the preamble of a decree.
As admitting the renderings God of gods and Judge of judges, and as a title of Christ.

outliers.reading: Takes the speaker of the psalm to be Christ himself, arguing from the God of gods that whatever beings are called gods were made so by the Word, and prefacing the exposition with a warning that God flatters no one.

themes: The mighty God, even the Lord, hath spoken, and called the earth from the rising of the sun unto the going down thereof.
Out of Zion, the perfection of beauty, God hath shined.
Our God shall come, and shall not keep silence: a fire shall devour before him, and it shall be very tempestuous round about him.
He shall call to the heavens from above, and to the earth, that he may judge his people.

5.pericope_label: Gather my saints together unto me; those that have made a covenant with me by sacrifice... Will I eat the flesh of bulls, or drink the blood of goats?

schools.summary: Treats the summons of the saints as among the book's most important verses, since it defines a term used throughout: the saints are those in the covenant, ratified by sacrifice. From this it draws the controlling conclusion that the psalm does not annul outward sacrifice but subordinates it, those censured being men who thought more of the rites than of the duties the covenant enjoined. It hears the heavens acknowledging God's right to arraign, restates that in modern terms as order in the physical world evidencing an ordered moral government, and proposes reading hills of oxen for a thousand hills, the received phrase having no analogy. A second voice notes the strengthened verb forms and the reach of the self-designation back to the commandments.
Hears Christ speaking the summons and extends the gathering through gospel ministers to the elect among the Gentiles. Notes why the bullock is named, as the chief beast used in sacrifice.

Reads the covenant-by-sacrifice clause as instruction, acquainting the people with the end of sacrifices as signs and seals and convicting them of trusting the outward act while neglecting its life and soul; takes the command itself as addressed to angels, and expects God to convince the people by thunders and storms rather than through priests or prophets. A second voice agrees the fault was never in the offering but in the manner, and then goes further than the rest: once the people trusted the sacrifices without looking to the thing signified, it was time to put them away — the precedent being the brazen serpent, broken to pieces when divine honours began to be paid to it.

Applies the address beyond Israel to the visible church in every age, declaring the futility of external worship where spiritual faith is absent, and restates the original contract by which God and people avouched one another. Puts the controversy historically: the fault was not that the institutions had been neglected but that the people took pride in them and hoped by their offerings to procure a dispensation for their lusts, as though sacrifice could excuse neglect of the law's weightier matters.

debates.question: Does the psalm abolish sacrifice or subordinate it?

positions.summary: Subordinate: every sacrifice witnessed to the covenant, and what is censured is valuing the rite above the duty.
Abolish, once trust was transferred to the rite itself — as the brazen serpent was destroyed when it began to receive divine honours.
Neither exactly: the institutions were kept but were being used as a purchase, offerings hoped to buy a dispensation for the offerer's sins.

debates.question: What does a thousand hills mean?

positions.summary: Nothing, as it stands: the phrase is literally mountains of a thousand, for which there is no analogy, and the Greek and Latin rightly read hills of oxen.
The received sense stands, the point being simply that all the beasts are already God's by creation and preservation.

outliers.reading: Treats one clause as a formal lexical definition governing the whole Psalter, holding that it fixes the sense of the word for saints wherever it occurs in the Hebrew hymn book.

themes: Gather my saints together unto me; those that have made a covenant with me by sacrifice.
And the heavens shall declare his righteousness: for God is judge himself. Selah.
Hear, O my people, and I will speak; O Israel, and I will testify against thee: I am God, even thy God.
I will not reprove thee for thy sacrifices or thy burnt offerings, to have been continually before me.
I will take no bullock out of thy house, nor he goats out of thy folds.
For every beast of the forest is mine, and the cattle upon a thousand hills.
I know all the fowls of the mountains: and the wild beasts of the field are mine.
If I were hungry, I would not tell thee: for the world is mine, and the fulness thereof.
Will I eat the flesh of bulls, or drink the blood of goats?

14.pericope_label: Offer unto God thanksgiving; and pay thy vows unto the most High... But unto the wicked God saith, What hast thou to do to declare my statutes, or that thou shouldest take my covenant in thy mouth?

schools.summary: Holds that gratitude and the performance of known duties are the ritual most pleasing to God, while denying that the verse implies any cessation of outward rites — only the subordination of form to spirit. At the turn it describes a shift to a worse class, men undisguisedly wicked who shelter under the covenant name, rendering the challenge as, how darest thou. A second voice insists that those addressed at the opening of the speech are not those addressed now, naming the accusation of the manifest sinners a distinct movement and correcting a scholar who ran them together.

Points out that thanksgiving is itself a sacrifice and records the saying that in the days of the Messiah every sacrifice will cease except praise, noting also a rendering that gives confession instead. Takes invocation to cover all religious worship and here prayer in particular, offered in faith and fervency and especially under affliction. Reads the division historically: the preceding verses concern godly Jews who believed in Christ but were still zealous of the law, these words the hypocrites among them — not openly profane sinners but men under a profession of religion, teachers who sat in Moses's chair and said and did not.

Ranks the sacrifices: what is indispensably required is first thankfulness, which does not consist barely in verbal acknowledgments but proceeds from a heart deeply affected with God's mercies, the vows being the substantial promises that were the soul of their sacrifices; prayer is a duty to be made conscience of, an acknowledgment of dependence. A second voice moves the other way and specifies the abolished rite exactly, listing what the thank-offering and the vow-offering consisted of, before saying what the whole system was for and that it now ends in the thing it signified; it names the wicked bluntly as the priests, Pharisees and scribes.

Draws the dividing line through the commandments: the earlier rebuke went to neglecters of the first table, this one to breakers of the second, and if lack of heart spoiled the worship of the more decent, how much more do open violations corrupt the sacrifices of the wicked. Challenges the profane but seemingly godly to show their title to the cloak of religion, notes how possible and common it is for men who declare God's statutes to live in disobedience to them, and warns that such usurpers will be thrust out as intruders.

debates.question: Does the psalm address one audience throughout or turn to a second group?

positions.summary: A distinct second group: those addressed at the opening of the speech are not those addressed here.
Two groups divided by which table of the law they break — the neglecters of the first, then the breakers of the second.
Two groups divided historically: godly Jews still zealous of the law, then the hypocrites among them.

debates.question: Who are the wicked the psalm now turns on?

positions.summary: Religious professionals specifically — the teachers, priests and scribes who declared the statutes without keeping them.
Anyone who practises iniquity while professing piety, and especially anyone who preaches it.
The manifestly wicked within the sanctuary itself, whose open violations disqualify them whatever their descent.

outliers.reading: Answers the psalm's displacement of ritual by specifying the ritual in full — the animals, the unleavened cakes mingled with oil, the wafers, the fried cakes of fine flour — and only then explains what the whole apparatus was for.

themes: Offer unto God thanksgiving; and pay thy vows unto the most High:
And call upon me in the day of trouble: I will deliver thee, and thou shalt glorify me.
But unto the wicked God saith, What hast thou to do to declare my statutes, or that thou shouldest take my covenant in thy mouth?

17.pericope_label: Seeing thou hatest instruction, and castest my words behind thee... Whoso offereth praise glorifieth me: and to him that ordereth his conversation aright will I shew the salvation of God

schools.summary: Works the indictment verb by verb: consenting means having pleasure in, giving the mouth to evil is letting it loose, framing deceit is weaving, sitting is better lurking, and slandering is literally giving a thrust — while mother's son marks a closer relation than brother where polygamy was practised. On the misread silence it states the mechanism, that God's forbearance is misconstrued until men think the divine Being as indifferent to evil as themselves. At the close it divides the final verse between the sincere formalist and the openly wicked, and, finding the received second clause hardly intelligible, canvasses two emendations to supply the mention of amendment the sense requires.

Takes the hated instruction as correction by the very statutes these men declared to others, and presses the identification of the thief-consenting hard: men who devoured widows' houses under pretence of long prayers, preferred a robber to Christ, and joined the thieves on the cross in reviling him. Reads the sitting concretely, in the chair of Moses or on the judgment seat, treats the recital of the charge as confirmation from one who saw every action, and defines the consideration asked for as repentance.

Keeps the historical frame — rapine and adulterous divines were common in that generation — and reads the silence as an eye continually upon them while judgment was withheld. Turns the appeal into a warning with a single exit, the iniquities marked down to be exhibited and none able to deliver but the Christ they reject; and on the last verse observes that the words are identical to those used earlier and should be read the same way. A second voice explains the misconstruction of patience as approbation, and reduces the closing promise to a line: such a man, and not the man who loads the altar, gives God the honour he requires.

Hears the closing appeal as entreaty rather than sentence, the Lord being loath to let even the most ungodly run on, and directs it at both classes at once, since those who trust in ceremonies and those who live in vice alike forget God; then defends the harshness of the threat, since God uses no soft words or velvet metaphors, nor may his servants when they speak of the wrath to come. Takes the received wording of the last verse as it stands, making holy living a choice evidence of salvation while cautioning that the best ordering of a life cannot save.

debates.question: What does the closing clause about ordering one's way mean?

positions.summary: Disposing one's way, or making that one's settled custom, on the received text and a manuscript variant.
Holy living as the evidence of salvation, the received wording standing as it is.
Neither, since the received text is hardly intelligible: read instead him who walks uprightly, or preferably him who has turned his way and changed his course of life.

debates.question: Do the two halves of the final verse address the same person?

positions.summary: No: the first clause is for the sincere formalist and the second for the openly wicked, which is why the second must speak of amendment.
Yes: one worshipper is described, offering praise and ordering his life, and to him the salvation is shown.

outliers.reading: Reads the general charge of consenting with a thief as a set of specific historical episodes from the gospels, matching each clause of the indictment to an act of the men he takes the psalm to be describing.

themes: Seeing thou hatest instruction, and castest my words behind thee.
When thou sawest a thief, then thou consentedst with him, and hast been partaker with adulterers.
Thou givest thy mouth to evil, and thy tongue frameth deceit.
Thou sittest and speakest against thy brother; thou slanderest thine own mother’s son.
These things hast thou done, and I kept silence; thou thoughtest that I was altogether such an one as thyself: but I will reprove thee, and set them in order before thine eyes.
Now consider this, ye that forget God, lest I tear you in pieces, and there be none to deliver.
Whoso offereth praise glorifieth me: and to him that ordereth his conversation aright will I shew the salvation of God.
